We decide what people are like very quickly, often in the first few seconds. The problem is that we describe our impression as if it were a fact. She is cold. He is arrogant. A more honest way to talk is to say how the person comes across. She comes across as a bit distant. He strikes me as very confident. These phrases leave a door open. They say this is what I see, not who the person really is. I use them all the time at work, especially with people I have just met. And I have noticed something. When I describe someone this way, I am much more willing to change my mind later. When I say he is arrogant, I stop looking. When I say he seems arrogant, I keep looking, and very often I find someone else.

My brother and I could not be more different. I am the talker in the family. He keeps to himself, and at parties he is usually in the kitchen, washing glasses, because it gives him something to do. People who meet him once think he is shy, or even a bit rude. He is neither. He is one of the most driven people I know. He started a small furniture business at forty, with no experience, and today it employs twelve people. He is also incredibly patient. When my daughter was learning to drive, I lasted one lesson. He took her out every Saturday for two months. If you want to know what he is like, do not listen to what he says. Watch what he does.

First, I say who the person is and how I know her: my sister, Paula. Then I describe my first impression: she comes across as quiet and a little serious. After that, I give a real quality: she strikes me as the most perceptive person in our family. Next, I prove it with an example: she always knows when something is wrong. In the end, I say how I feel about her, and why we click.
